title: Police Chief takes issue with media report on recent death in custody
article: Winnipeg Police Chief Danny Smyth says he is "disappointed, but not surprised" by a media report that he felt misrepresented police actions in a recent death in custody being investigated by the Independent Investigation Unit of Manitoba, the province's police watchdog.

In a post on the Winnipeg Police's Tried and True blog last Thursday, Smyth was responding to a CBC Manitoba report which interviewed two witnesses who shared a one-minute video showing a man on the ground and what appear to be two police officers pinning him down near the intersection of Sherbook Street and Broadway, leaving them "stunned."
Smyth criticized that CBC Manitoba chose to report the incident using the perspective of two people who witnessed and recorded just part of the encounter.

"The event, as reported by CBC Manitoba, was interpreted through the narrow focus of these two people who had no first-hand experience with police use-of-force encounters," said Smyth in the blog. "There was no context provided that explained what led up to the encounter, but descriptors of "police violence" and "police beating" were readily used in the report. To be clear, I am not critical of the two witnesses who came forward. I have no doubt the information that they provide to the investigators, once they are interviewed, will assist the investigation, but they are just two of many, many witnesses that will help the IIU determine what occurred."

Winnipeg Police reported that on Oct. 15, at just before 11 p.m., officers were called to the Broadway and Sherbrook area for the report of a man in distress running into traffic and acting erratically. Attending officers located the man, and he was taken into custody. He went into medical distress and was rushed to Health Sciences Centre in critical condition, and was later pronounced dead.
The IIU was notified and assumed responsibility for the investigation. In a release, IIU said during the arrest the male began to have trouble breathing.

At a press conference last Tuesday on an unrelated matter, a Winnipeg Police spokesperson acknowledged that they were aware of the video but referred to the previous day's police statement and that it was now an IIU matter.

In the blog, Smyth said officers responded after a woman called 911 for help and that officers were told a man had jumped in front of the woman's vehicle, started punching her window and tried to enter it. The woman indicated there was blood on her car, Smyth wrote. Police were also called by a second caller who was concerned about the man's behaviour.

The man was later identified by a spokesperson for the Webequie First Nation - located almost 550 kilometres north of Thunder Bay - as Elias Whitehead. Family, friends and community members held a vigil Thursday evening at the Shell gas station on Sherbrook and Broadway, near where the incident took place.

"A competent, well-trained, and professional police service that is accountable to the community it serves, is in the public's interest," said Smyth. "The media has a role by ensuring accountability through balanced and objective inquiry. That too is in everyone's interest. It appears in this instance, some media publications have chosen very different approaches about the interests they serve. And for that reason, you will find us taking a different approach when it comes to the media and IIU matters. We owe it to the public to ensure the basic facts are available at the outset."
